title: (Scenario) You deploy a new version that writes data in a new format, then discover a bug and need to roll back — why can't you simply deploy the old binary (the old code may not understand the new data), and what is the expand-and-contract principle for safe rollback (ensure old and new versions can coexist throughout the migration)?
shortTitle: Why can't you simply deploy the old binary after writing data in a new format, and what is expand-and-contract?

s1_definition.profdef: When a new version writes data in a new format and you then redeploy the old binary, the old code encounters data written in a shape it was never programmed to read — a new column it ignores but depends on, a changed type it misparses, or a field whose meaning changed — so it may crash, return wrong results, or corrupt further data. The rollback restores the code but not a data format the code understands. Expand-and-contract (also known as parallel-change) is the discipline that makes rollback safe: you split a breaking change into an expand phase where you add the new format additively while continuing to produce the old format so old and new code can coexist, a long coexistence phase where both versions run against compatible data, and a contract phase, performed only after you are fully confident and will not roll back, where you finally remove the old format. During the entire window before contract, either binary can run against the data, so rolling back is always safe.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India switches its account ledger to a new format overnight. If a problem appears and they bring back yesterday's clerk, he opens the ledger and cannot read a single entry — the format is foreign to him — so he cannot serve anyone. Expand-and-contract is the safe way: first the bank writes every entry in both the old format and the new format side by side for a long period, so whether today's clerk or yesterday's clerk is on duty, each can read the entries they understand. Only after the bank is completely sure the new format is correct and they will never need the old clerk again do they stop writing the old format. Throughout the risky period, either clerk can work, so going back is always safe.
s1_definition.oneliner: The old binary cannot read data written in a new format, so you keep both formats alive through expand (add new, keep old), coexist, and only contract (remove old) once rollback is no longer needed.

sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the team changes how transfer amounts are stored, from a decimal rupees field to an integer paise field. They deploy the new version, it writes new rows in the new format, and then a bug is discovered.

Problem 1 — a naive cutover stopped writing the old decimal field, so after rolling back the old binary reads null or zero amounts and serves wrong balances. The code reverted; the data did not.

Problem 2 — the team needs a way where rolling back the code always lands on data the old code understands, no matter when the rollback happens.

The fix applies expand-and-contract: in the expand phase the service dual-writes both the decimal and the paise fields; during coexistence either binary can read its format and a verifier confirms they agree; the contract phase, which drops the decimal field, is deferred until the team is certain. The mini-project builds a `Row` with both fields, an `ExpandPhaseService` that dual-writes, a `Verifier` that checks agreement, a simulated old-binary read that succeeds during expand and would fail after a naive cutover, and a `ContractPhase` that is only invoked after confidence. The demo shows a clean rollback during the expand phase.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: one transfer of fifty thousand rupees, written by the new version, followed by a rollback during the expand phase, and later a contract step.

Step 1 — Expand, dual-write. The new version writes the transfer in both formats: the old decimal amount of fifty thousand and the new paise amount of five million. Both fields are populated.

Step 2 — Verify agreement. The verifier checks that the paise field equals the decimal field times one hundred, finds they agree, and confirms the formats are consistent. This agreement is the precondition for ever contracting.

Step 3 — Bug found, roll back during expand. A bug is discovered in the new version, so the team rolls back to the old binary. The old binary reads the old decimal amount field, which is still populated because the expand phase never stopped writing it, and returns the correct fifty thousand. The rollback is completely safe.

Step 4 — Contract gated off. The contract phase is attempted with the safety latch off, so it refuses to drop the old format and logs that rollback is still safe. The old format remains, so the system can keep rolling back for as long as needed.

Step 5 — Contract later, point of no return. Much later, after the new version has run cleanly and confidence is high, the contract phase is allowed and drops the old decimal field. From this moment the old binary would read a null amount and break, which is exactly why the contract was deliberately deferred until rollback was no longer required.

```
2026-10-24 19:22:10 [INFO] Dual-write TRF-1 amount=50000 minor=5000000
2026-10-24 19:22:10 [INFO] Formats agree? true
2026-10-24 19:22:10 [WARNING] Bug found → rolling back to old binary (expand phase)
2026-10-24 19:22:10 [INFO] OLD BINARY reads TRF-1 amount=Rs.50000
2026-10-24 19:22:10 [WARNING] Contract NOT allowed yet — old format retained, rollback still safe
2026-10-24 19:22:10 [INFO] Still safe to roll back; contract deferred until full confidence
2026-10-24 19:22:10 [INFO] === Later: confidence high, perform contract ===
2026-10-24 19:22:10 [WARNING] CONTRACT: dropped old format for TRF-1 (no rollback after this)
2026-10-24 19:22:10 [SEVERE] OLD BINARY BROKEN: TRF-1 amount is NULL
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  New version deploy → write transfer
    │
    ▼ EXPAND: dual-write
    amount=50000 (OLD)  +  amount_minor=5000000 (NEW)
    │
    ▼ Verify: 5000000 == 50000 × 100 → agree
    │
    ├─ bug found → ROLL BACK old binary
    │     reads amount=50000 (OLD intact) → CORRECT, safe
    │
    ▼ COEXIST (days/weeks): both formats maintained, backfill history
    │
    ▼ CONTRACT (much later, gated): drop amount (OLD)
      old binary would read NULL → BROKEN → which is why contract waits
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Expand-and-Contract Rollout ═══

  ┌────────────┐ deploy ┌──────────────────┐
  │ CI/CD      │───────→│ Service          │  canary → full, feature-flagged
  └────────────┘        └────────┬─────────┘
                        EXPAND: dual-write (old + new)
                                 ▼
                     ┌────────────────────────┐
                     │ PostgreSQL              │  amount + amount_minor (additive)
                     └──────────┬──────────────┘
                                │ Verifier (continuous: old == new)
                                ▼
                     ┌────────────────────────┐
                     │ Backfill Worker         │  history → new format, throttled
                     └────────────────────────┘

  COEXIST window = either binary can run against the data = rollback always safe.
  CONTRACT = separate later deploy, DROP old column, gated by a safety latch.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Parallel-Change (Expand/Contract) ═══

  ┌─ Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Parallel-Change: expand (add+dual-write), coexist, contract│
  │ Verification gate: contract only after formats agree       │
  │ Safety latch / feature flag: contract explicitly enabled   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: ExpandService writes; Verifier checks; Contract removes │
  │ O: new format added, old path untouched during expand      │
  │ D: phases depend on Row abstraction, not storage details   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌────────────────────┐ writes ┌────────┐ reads ┌──────────────────┐
  │ ExpandPhaseService │───────▶│ Row    │◀──────│ OldBinaryReader  │
  │ + writeTransfer()  │        │ amount │       │ + read()         │
  └────────────────────┘        │ minor  │       └──────────────────┘
  ┌──────────┐ gate  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Verifier │──────▶│ ContractPhase│ (deferred, latched)
  └──────────┘       └──────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: format lifecycle ──
  [OLD ONLY] ──expand (add+dual-write)──→ [BOTH] ──verify + confidence──→ [NEW ONLY]
                     │ rollback safe here           │ contract = point of no return
                     └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (safe rollback) ──
  1. service.writeTransfer(TRF-1, 50000) → amount + amount_minor
  2. verifier.agrees(row) → true
  3. rollback → oldBinary.read(row) → 50000 (OLD intact) → safe
  4. contract gated off → old format retained
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The reason I cannot simply deploy the old binary after the new version has written data in a new format is that code and data have different lifecycles. When I redeploy, the code reverts instantly and completely, but the data does not — every row the new version wrote while it was live stays in the new format. So the old binary, which assumes the old format, now reads rows that violate its assumptions. Sometimes that fails loudly with a crash or a parse error, but the more dangerous case is a quiet failure where the old code reads a field whose meaning changed and silently produces wrong financial results, while the team believes they are safely back on a known-good version.

Expand-and-contract, also called parallel-change, is the discipline that makes rollback genuinely safe, and it works by never having a moment during the risky window where only one format exists. In the expand phase I make only additive schema changes — add the new column or table, build indexes online — and I have the application dual-write, so every change is written in both the old and the new format. Because the old format is still being maintained, the old binary can be redeployed at any time and will read correct data. Then comes the coexistence phase, which is the heart of the safety: for days or weeks the new code runs but keeps producing the old format, I verify continuously that the two formats agree, and I backfill historical rows into the new format in throttled restartable batches. If the new version has a bug, I roll back and the old binary just works, because the old format was never abandoned.

Only when confidence is high — the new version has run cleanly, verification shows perfect agreement, and I am certain I will not need to roll back — do I enter the contract phase, where I stop dual-writing, drop the old column, and switch reads fully to the new format. That is the one irreversible step, and I deliberately do it as a separate, much later deployment, because it is precisely the moment rollback stops being safe. I treat the contract as its own change with its own review, because folding it into the initial rollout is exactly what recreates the trap of an un-rollbackable deploy.

In my banking work this was how we changed amount storage from decimal rupees to integer paise with full rollback safety. We dual-wrote both fields, verified they agreed on every transfer, kept the old field alive for weeks so any rollback landed on data the old binary understood, backfilled history in the background, and only dropped the old column long after the rollout had proven itself. And the same discipline applies beyond database schemas — to API shapes, event schemas, file formats, and cache layouts — always the same three phases. The principle I take into interviews is that the goal is to always have a window where both the previous and the current version can run against the same state, because that window is the only thing that turns rollback from a hope into a real, exercised option.
